title: 7.17.1 Playtest and reflect: Breakout
description: Play your finished Breakout with the mouse and with the keys, try to break it, find one surprise, link it to your code and choose one change. AI-graded with hints.

aiGrader.prompt:
Everything you need is in 7.13.1 (Plan: Break Breakout into parts) and 7.16.2 (Lab: Pick a mode): go back and reread them if you get stuck. A few short sentences per answer is plenty, in your own everyday words.

Play your finished Breakout at least twice, once with the mouse and once with the arrow keys. Try to break it: catch the ball on the very ends of the paddle, slide the paddle into the ball from the side, let the ball fall out on purpose. Then answer:

1. How many times did you play, and how did it go?

2. What is one thing that surprised you or did not work as you expected?

3. Which part of your code do you think that comes from?

4. What is one rule or number you would change, and what would it do to the game?

rubric.title: Says how many times they played and how it went
rubric.description: The student says they played, or gives any detail of a play (a score, bricks cleared, lives lost, which control they used, a way it went wrong). Any mention of playing earns full credit. Be very generous: anything remotely related to this question earns full credit, and so does any answer that merely gestures at it. Read the student's whole response, not only the line that answers this question: if anything anywhere in it touches this question, even indirectly, give full credit. Do not mark this criterion missing just because the student skipped this numbered question: when the response is about their Breakout game at all, even if it only describes the game or says how they feel about it, mark this criterion met. Only a blank response, or one about something else entirely, is a miss.

rubric.title: Names one thing that surprised or broke
rubric.description: The student names anything that surprised them, felt wrong or did not work as expected, however small. If they found nothing, saying so or naming something they tried earns full credit too. Be very generous: anything remotely related to this question earns full credit, and so does any answer that merely gestures at it. Read the student's whole response, not only the line that answers this question: if anything anywhere in it touches this question, even indirectly, give full credit. Do not mark this criterion missing just because the student skipped this numbered question: when the response is about their Breakout game at all, even if it only describes the game or says how they feel about it, mark this criterion met. Only a blank response, or one about something else entirely, is a miss.

rubric.title: Says which part of the code that touches
rubric.description: The student connects what they saw to some part of the game or its code, such as moveBall, the paddle bounce, the steering line, hitAt, the edge tests in hitBricks, checkEnd or pickMode, even loosely or wrongly. Any guess at a cause earns full credit. Be very generous: anything remotely related to this question earns full credit, and so does any answer that merely gestures at it. Read the student's whole response, not only the line that answers this question: if anything anywhere in it touches this question, even indirectly, give full credit. Do not mark this criterion missing just because the student skipped this numbered question: when the response is about their Breakout game at all, even if it only describes the game or says how they feel about it, mark this criterion met. Only a blank response, or one about something else entirely, is a miss.

rubric.title: Names one rule they would change and what it would do
rubric.description: The student names one rule, number or feature to change or add, and anything about what it would do to the game. Any idea earns full credit. Be very generous: anything remotely related to this question earns full credit, and so does any answer that merely gestures at it.
